summary: Fixes a problem in ICE where an agent may run out of candidate pairs to check and conclude that connectivity has failed, even though more candidates could still be discovered. The document makes agents wait a little longer before giving up. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Imagine giving up on finding your friend because the first places you checked were empty, though a hint was still on its way. This document tells the program to be patient a little longer before saying it failed.

questions: why does ice fail too early
what is the pac timer in ice
how long should an ice agent wait before failing
subtitle: Why ICE should wait a little longer before declaring failure, and how the PAC timer does it.

tldr.problem: An ICE agent can run out of candidate pairs to check and declare failure immediately, before it has had time to discover peer-reflexive candidates that would have led to a working connection.
tldr.mechanism: The agent starts a PAC timer when connectivity checks begin and does not move a checklist from Running to Failed while it runs. The recommended duration is the connectivity check transaction timeout, 39.5 seconds with default values.
tldr.outcome: ICE no longer fails too early in common cases. In cases where ICE should fail, it now fails only when the timer expires. The RFC updates RFC 8445 and RFC 8838.

today: RFC 8863 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 8445 and RFC 8838.

sections.title: The Premature Failure Problem
sections.content:
ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment, RFC 8445) is a protocol for NAT traversal for UDP-based communication. Endpoints exchange candidates, form a list of candidate pairs, and test each pair. If all pairs fail, the overall ICE process is usually considered failed.

The catch is that successful inbound checks from the remote peer can create new candidates, called peer-reflexive candidates. These form new pairs that are tested like any other. If an endpoint runs out of pairs before learning of such candidates, it declares failure too soon and ends ICE processing.

This RFC simply requires an ICE agent to wait a minimum amount of time before declaring failure, even when no pairs are left to check or all have failed.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a new clue shows up after you have already run out of places to look. The fix is to wait a bit before giving up.

sections.title: When the Problem Occurs
sections.content:
In most ICE scenarios, the long timeouts for connectivity check transactions, typically tens of seconds, hide the problem. Three specific cases make it frequent.

  • No candidates from the peer. Under RFC 8838 an agent may provide zero candidates, for example when it knows the other side is directly reachable. Following RFC 8445 strictly, the peer's checklist is empty and ICE fails at once.
  • All candidates discarded. The peer may discard candidates it cannot use, such as a host candidate with an IPv6 address in a NAT64 scenario. The checklist is empty again.
  • Immediate candidate pair failure. Some pairs fail well before the transaction timeout, for example a check to a non-routable address that gets an immediate ICMP error. The checklist may hold only failed pairs.
sections.eli5: It happens when you were given no places to look, when the places you were given are no good, or when every place you try says no right away.

sections.title: The PAC Timer
sections.content:
When a full ICE implementation begins ICE processing, it MUST set a PAC timer (Patiently Awaiting Connectivity) so ICE runs for a minimum time before determining failure. The agent starts it once it believes connectivity checks are starting: it has sent the values needed for checks (such as the username fragment and password) and has some sign that the remote side is ready. It starts the timer even if it has sent or received no candidates.

The RECOMMENDED duration equals the agent's connectivity check transaction timeout including all retransmissions. With default retransmission timeout (RTO) and Rc values this is 39.5 seconds, as explained in RFC 5389. The value is described as an educated guess, since the agent does not know how many pairs or what pacing the remote side uses. The application is best placed to decide what is reasonable.

While the timer runs, the agent MUST NOT change a checklist from Running to Failed, even if no pairs are left, so it will not remove data streams or set the ICE session to Failed. When the timer expires, the agent MUST resume normal processing, including setting checklists with no pairs left to Failed.

A consequence is that where ICE should fail, such as when both sides give candidates with unsupported address families, it now fails only when the PAC timer expires. The RFC expects minimal application impact.
sections.eli5: The program sets a timer, like an egg timer. Until it rings, the program is not allowed to say it failed, even if it has nothing left to try.

sections.title: Nomination and Trickle ICE
sections.content:
The PAC timer also bears on nomination, the choice of the final candidate pair (RFC 8445, Section 8.1.1). That RFC sets no minimum time before nominating, but to pick the best pair, ICE needs enough time to find and check peer-reflexive candidates. The controlling agent SHOULD wait a sufficient time before nominating pairs and MAY use the PAC timer for this. It keeps full discretion and MAY nominate earlier.

Trickle ICE (RFC 8838) waits for an end-of-candidates indication before declaring failure. But peer-reflexive candidates can still appear after that indication, so the PAC timer MUST still be used with Trickle ICE. Since sending end-of-candidates is only a SHOULD, agents need a backup such as a timer, and they MAY use the PAC timer as that fallback.
sections.eli5: The timer also helps the program pick the best path, since better paths may show up a little later. It can also stand in when the other side forgets to say it is done sending clues.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: The security considerations for ICE are in RFC 8445. This specification only recommends that agents wait for a period before they declare ICE failure, and it adds no new security considerations. It has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Waiting a little longer does not open any new doors for trouble, so there is nothing new to worry about.

items.title: No candidates from peer
items.text: The peer sent zero candidates, so the checklist is empty.

items.title: All candidates discarded
items.text: The peer cannot use the candidates, for example an unsupported address family.

items.title: Immediate pair failure
items.text: Pairs fail at once, for example on an ICMP error.
